title: Overspent This Diwali? A Sober Plan to Clear Festive Card Debt
excerpt: Card debt at over 40% a year is the most expensive money in the house. Here is the order to tackle it: total it, pay above the minimum, then move what remains to cheaper money.
body:
• Credit-card finance charges in India can run over 40% a year, while personal loans start from about 10.99% a year — so festive card debt left rolling is the most expensive money most households owe.
  • The standard routes out, in order: total every due first, pay well above the minimum with a target clearance date, then compare a balance transfer against consolidating into a single personal loan at the shortest tenure you can afford.
  • The 2026 context: card spending hit Rs 2.04 lakh crore in September and was expected to rise to Rs 2.28-2.38 lakh crore in October as festive sales began, according to CareEdge Ratings figures reported by Hindu BusinessLine.
  • Banks run Financial Literacy and Credit Counselling Centres (FLCCs) that can help negotiate interest relief — a free first call before paying any debt-relief company.

Diwali fell on November 8 this year, and for many households the festival's real bill arrives with the November card statement. The pattern is well documented: CareEdge Ratings data reported by Hindu BusinessLine put credit-card spending at Rs 2.04 lakh crore in September 2026, with Rs 2.28-2.38 lakh crore expected in October as festive sales began. What turns a festive splurge into a problem is not the spending — it is the interest rate on whatever is not paid off.

Know the rate you are actually paying

Credit-card finance charges in India can go over 40% per annum, Paisabazaar's post-Diwali debt guide notes, while personal loan rates start from about 10.99% per annum. That gap is the whole strategy: every rupee of card balance you can move to cheaper money, or clear outright, stops compounding at the punitive rate. The same arithmetic is why advisers insist a card is a payment instrument, not a borrowing one. As Outlook Money put it in its November festive-finance guide: if the full bill cannot be paid on the due date, the purchase is unaffordable.

The routes out, compared

Balance transfer. Move the outstanding balance to a card offering a lower or teaser rate, or take the transfer on EMI, if you can realistically clear it in the near future without a separate loan. Personal loan consolidation. Roll card debt and small loans into one personal loan; choose the shortest tenure you can afford, since a higher EMI still costs less in total interest, and a good credit score or an existing bank relationship may win a lower rate. Top-up loan. If you already have a home or personal loan, a top-up at the rate you are already paying usually needs less documentation than a fresh loan. Family. Borrowing from friends or relatives works only with a stated repayment timeline — and taking a refusal gracefully. Counselling. Banks' Financial Literacy and Credit Counselling Centres, often staffed by former branch managers, may help secure interest reductions or relief on punitive charges.

"Festivals should create memories, not EMIs."

— Outlook Money, festive finance guide, November 2026

Before next Diwali

The same Outlook Money guidance, with answers from Col. Sanjeev Govila (retd), CEO of Hum Fauji Initiatives, among others, sets the preventive version: fix a total festive budget from income and savings without touching the emergency fund or carrying a card balance, split it into buckets — gifts, celebrations, travel, personal — with a per-person gift amount set in advance, and stop when a bucket is empty. The foundations underneath are unglamorous: health insurance, roughly six months of expenses in an emergency fund, and no expensive debt carried into the season. None of that helps with this month's statement — but the consolidation maths above does, and it starts with one honest total of everything owed.

Set a target clearance date; the minimum due barely touches principal at 40%-plus annual charges.
